# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# A Careful Read of the Varga and Holm Comment

**Bottom line:** Sections 1–5 are a valuable, mostly well-documented re-analysis. The attrition finding in particular is a serious and new problem for the Halden paper. The conclusion, however, goes beyond the comment's own evidence. After every correction it can make, a gain of about 11% in output per actual hour remains. The "entirely an artifact" claim rests on a novelty argument that the authors assert rather than test, and it sets aside randomised evidence they themselves cite as reliable.

## 1. Arithmetic: mostly right, with two inconsistencies

**Correct:**
- Table 2:
  - 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%.
  - 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%.
  - 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- Hours ratios: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861.
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a fall of about 2.6%.

**Inconsistent:**
- **The hours breakdown does not add up.** Thirty-two scheduled hours, plus 0.7 extra hours on each of four days (2.8), plus 1.6 hours on the day off, gives about **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Reaching 34.6 would need only about 0.25 extra hours per day. Either the breakdown uses a different base or one figure is wrong. This matters because the hours correction carries much of the argument.
- **The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD per month. At that rate, the remaining 0.29 SD runs out at around **month 8.7**, not month ten. This hardly helps the authors' case. The bigger problem is that a straight line through two points is not a basis for prediction at all (section 3).

## 2. What the comment gets right

- **Attrition (section 1)** is the most important finding.
  - The working paper's statement that withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" appears to be inaccurate.
  - Seven of the nine organisations withdrew after the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or output.
  - This is outcome-related attrition, and the original authors should answer for it.
- **Record-based output (section 2)** turns my earlier "managers may rate optimistically" concern into a measured gap. The manager's index was higher in 19 of 23 organisations, by 3.8 points on average.
- **Actual hours (section 3)** quantifies the scheduled-hours problem. Hours fell 14%, not 20%. This closely matches Varden's case-processing figure of 13%, which is reassuring.
- **Revenue (section 4)** is right that a nominal comparison flatters the result.
- **Sectoral claims (section 5)** is right that the per-hour metric makes "gains in every sector" close to automatic.
- **The data note** is candid that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## 3. The central overreach: "entirely an artifact"

**The comment's own numbers leave a gain.** Correcting for measurement and hours takes the gain from 23.4% to 10.8%, not to zero. Two things are then needed to reach "entirely":

- **Attrition is not quantified.** The comment shows that withdrawals were plausibly negative but provides no outcome data or bounds for the nine organisations. Even if each had output equal to the retail record-based figure, nine of 70 would not remove an 11% gain on their own. The comment should have estimated bounds rather than implying the gain disappears.
- **Novelty is asserted, not tested.**
  - The evidence offered is an energy measure, not output, at two time points, extrapolated in a straight line.
  - The Halden output index was collected **monthly**, and the authors had the microdata. They could have checked directly whether output per hour fell between months 1 and 6. A falling trend would be strong support for the novelty argument, and a flat one would weaken it. The comment does not report it.
  - "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a debating move, not a finding. The defensible conclusion is that durability is **unknown**, not that the effect is zero.

**The abstract and data note do not match the conclusion.** The abstract says the four problems account for "most" of the gain. The conclusion says "entirely." The data note says the corrected estimates describe only non-random subsets. Yet the conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole, not just to the Halden pilot.

## 4. Varden is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But the same randomised trial found **+12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing offices** (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). That trial:

- used administrative records, not manager ratings, so it addresses the output-measure problem;
- used timesheet hours, so it addresses the denominator problem;
- randomised with a concurrent control group, so it addresses selection and attrition;
- measured at nine months, longer than Halden's six, which partly addresses novelty.

The comment's corrected Halden estimate (+10.8%) and Varden's estimate (+12.5%) come from different designs and different settings, and they **converge**. That convergence is the strongest evidence in the three documents against "entirely an artifact." The comment never mentions it.

The negative counter-office result is real. But it shows that reduced hours fail in coverage-bound work. It does not show that per-hour gains are illusory everywhere.

## 5. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden paper

- **The Varden authors had already said all of this.** They stated that the analysis was unregistered, that it rested on seven offices, and that "a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism." They also registered a confirmatory test. The comment criticises a claim the Varden paper does not make.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known" is not accurate as stated.** Meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month outcomes existed. The analysis itself may well be post hoc, but the data were not chosen with the results in view.
- **A double standard.** The comment rejects a seven-office correlation as a mechanism, then offers its own novelty mechanism based on extrapolating two points from a survey. Both should be treated as hypotheses.
- **The two explanations are compatible.** The meetings hypothesis is not an alternative to the comment's scepticism about rest. It suggests the gain comes from removing low-value time, not from better-rested staff. That is a real gain, but one that might not need shorter hours, and it fits much of the comment's broader view.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Record-based output has its own bias.** "Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types. That measures hours, not output, so it falls almost automatically when hours are cut. It would bias the record-based index downward for professional services. The comment should show results with and without hours-type records.
- **The retail record-based fall rests on three organisations.** It is suggestive at best.
- **CPI is a crude deflator for business revenue.** Sector price indices would be better. There is also no comparison group, so a real fall of 2.6% may simply track the wider economy. The authors admit revenue is a weak proxy.
- **The 17-organisation subset may be unusual.** Organisations with both time tracking and output records are likely more measurement-minded. The bias could run either way.
- **The recommendations are sound.** Record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, an 18-month or longer follow-up, and analysis of all enrolled organisations are all sensible.

## What the comment can fairly claim

The Halden headline of +23.4% is substantially overstated. Optimistic manager ratings, scheduled-hours denominators and possibly outcome-related attrition together roughly halve it, leaving about +11% in a non-random subset. Halden's conclusion that the model is "sector-general" is not supported. The durability of the remaining gain is uncertain.

The comment cannot fairly claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact." That claim needs:

- an analysis of the monthly output trend,
- bounds on the attrition effect,
- an explanation of why Varden's randomised case-processing result, which agrees with the comment's own corrected estimate, should be dismissed.

## Where the three documents leave things

- **Coverage-bound work:** Reduced hours lower output and service. The two studies agree on this, and it is the most consistent finding.
- **Backlog-style knowledge work:**
  - Output per actual hour rises by roughly 10–13%. Two independent estimates support this.
  - Actual hours fall by roughly 13–14%, not 20%.
  - Output per employee is near flat or slightly down.
- **Unresolved:**
  - whether the gain lasts beyond 6–9 months;
  - how much of it comes from cutting meetings and process waste rather than rest;
  - the effect on cost per unit of output, which none of the documents measure.
